chapters.title: Chapter 0: Learning Objective
chapters.content:
Module goal

Build clear retail domain foundations before deeper technical or AI implementation.

Learning Objective

By the end of this module, learners should be able to:

  • Explain how a retail business operates end-to-end
  • Identify major retail systems and their responsibilities
  • Understand how data flows through retail operations
  • Describe store hierarchy and ownership structures
  • Recognize POS dependencies and failure impact

What You Will Learn, Chapter By Chapter

ChapterTopicKey question it answers
1What is Retail?What does a retailer actually do besides selling?
2Retail Value ChainHow do product and money travel from supplier to finance?
3Retail Organization HierarchyWho owns what, from the whole chain down to one terminal?
4Retail Systems LandscapeWhich system is responsible for which job?
5POS DependenciesWhat breaks when something POS relies on fails?
6Online vs Offline vs OmnichannelWhy is mixing channels harder to run?
7Business KPIsHow do we measure whether retail operations are healthy?
8-11Scenario, Quiz, Assignments, CompletionCan you apply what you learned?

Outcome Standard

You are ready for Module 2 when you can trace one transaction from supplier inventory creation through checkout, payment settlement, and finance posting without ambiguity.

How To Study This Module

  • Focus first on process sequence, then on system ownership.
  • Learn incident impact in business terms, not only technical terms.
  • Memorize where data is mastered vs where it is consumed.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the focus of Module 1 in one line?
checkpoint.answer: Build clear retail domain foundations before deeper technical or AI implementation.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: What is Retail?
chapters.content:
Definition

Retail

Retail is the business of selling products or services directly to consumers.

Examples:

WalmartTargetCostcoKrogerHEBAmazon Fresh

A Retailer Does More Than Sell

A retail company performs much more than selling goods.

A retail company does much more than billing. It sources products, stores inventory, transports products, sells to customers, collects payment, and reconciles finances.

It must:

  1. Source products
  2. Store inventory
  3. Transport products
  4. Sell to customers
  5. Collect payment
  6. Reconcile finances

Retail Is A Coordinated Network

A customer sees one bill at checkout, but the business depends on synchronized operations across merchandising, supply chain, store execution, finance, and digital channels.

Core Operating Risks

RiskWhat goes wrong
Demand mismatchOverstock creates carrying cost, understock creates lost sales.
Price integrity gapsWrong price or missing promotion erodes trust.
Execution varianceStore-level process inconsistency impacts service quality.
Settlement delayRecognized sales may not equal cash received same day.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is retail not just billing at POS?
checkpoint.answer: Because billing is one step in the full chain from sourcing to settlement and accounting.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Retail Value Chain
chapters.content:
End-to-End Retail Flow

  1. Supplier
  2. Distribution Center
  3. Warehouse
  4. Store
  5. POS Checkout
  6. Payment Processor
  7. Settlement
  8. Finance Systems
Important distinction:

Sale completed ≠ Money settled

Detailed Explanation

1. Supplier

Manufactures products.

Manufactures products and sends master data.

Details
Examples
  • Coca-Cola
  • Nestlé
  • PepsiCo
Outputs:
  • Product inventory
  • Product master data

2. Distribution Center (DC)

Central hub for inventory.

Details
Responsibilities
  • Receive supplier shipments
  • Aggregate inventory
  • Route inventory to stores
KPIs:
  • Inventory turnover
  • Order fulfillment rate

3. Warehouse Operations

Details
Tracks
  • On-hand inventory
  • Reserved inventory
  • Damaged inventory
Systems Used:
  • WMS (Warehouse Management System)

4. Store Operations

Stocking, receiving, cycle counting, customer service.

Details
Activities:
  • Shelf stocking
  • Product receiving
  • Cycle counting
  • Customer service
Store Metrics:
  • Sales per hour
  • Stock availability
  • Shrinkage

5. Checkout

Customer purchases items.

Flow:

  1. Scan Item
  2. Lookup Product
  3. Apply Price
  4. Apply Promotion
  5. Calculate Tax
  6. Payment
  7. Receipt

Primary System: POS

6. Settlement

After payment:

  1. Customer Card
  2. Payment Processor
  3. Bank
  4. Retailer Account

Settlement may occur later than checkout.

Fund movement after checkout through payment network and bank.

Where Delays Commonly Occur

StepFrequent Delay CauseBusiness Effect
Supplier -> DCLate ASN or shipment mismatchReceiving backlog, shelf gaps
Store -> POSCatalog or price feed lagManual overrides at checkout
Payment -> SettlementBatch timing or processor holdCashflow visibility delay
Key point

Retail success depends on both physical product flow and digital data flow. Break either one and customer experience degrades quickly.

checkpoint.prompt: What comes after POS checkout in money movement?
checkpoint.answer: Processor and banking settlement flow, then finance posting.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Retail Organization Hierarchy
chapters.content:
Most large retailers follow a hierarchy.

Example

  1. Retail Chain
  2. Region
  3. District / Cluster
  4. Store
  5. POS Terminal
LevelWhat it isExample:Notes
Retail ChainEntire business.HEBEntire business
RegionGeographical grouping.
  • Texas South
  • Texas Central
  • Texas North
Geographic grouping
Cluster / DistrictA manager may oversee multiple stores.District 48Manager oversees many stores
StorePhysical location.Store #245Address, hours, manager, inventory
TerminalPoint of sale workstation.
  • POS 7
  • POS 12
  • POS 16
Scans items, takes tenders, prints receipts

Store Attributes:

  • Address
  • Opening hours
  • Store manager
  • Inventory

Terminal Responsibilities:

  • Scan items
  • Process tenders
  • Print receipts

Operational Ownership By Level

LevelOwns
ChainEnterprise standards, platform strategy, vendor contracts.
RegionExecution consistency, regional demand shape, escalations.
DistrictMulti-store coaching, incident triage coordination.
StoreDaily operations, labor allocation, service quality.
TerminalTransaction execution and immediate customer interaction.

Incident Blast Radius

Where the issue isWho is affected
TerminalOne checkout lane
StoreAll lanes in one location
RegionDozens of stores simultaneously
Why it matters

Hierarchy determines blast radius, owner routing, and escalation urgency.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does hierarchy matter for incidents?
checkpoint.answer: It determines blast radius, owner routing, and escalation urgency.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Retail Systems Landscape
chapters.content:
Retail operations depend on multiple systems.

Core System Map

ERP
|
|
IMS -------- POS -------- CRM
| | |
| | |
OMS ------- Loyalty ---- Payments

System-By-System Guide

SystemPurposeDetails
POS (Point of Sale)Execute retail transactions.

Functions:

  • Scan items
  • Price calculation
  • Tax calculation
  • Discounts
  • Tender processing

Examples:

  • NCR
  • Toshiba
  • Oracle XStore
OMS (Order Management System)Manage customer orders.

Examples:

  • Buy Online Pickup In Store (BOPIS)
  • Curbside pickup
  • Delivery orders
IMS (Inventory Management System)Track inventory quantity.

Tracks:

  • Available stock
  • Reserved stock
  • Damaged stock
  • In-transit stock
ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning)Business accounting and finance.

Examples:

  • SAP
  • Oracle ERP

Responsible for:

  • Financial posting
  • Procurement
  • Accounting
CRM (Customer Relationship Management)Manage customer relationships.

Stores:

  • Customer profiles
  • Purchase history
  • Marketing preferences
Loyalty SystemReward repeat customers.

Examples:

  • Membership points
  • Coupons
  • Personalized offers
Payment SystemProcess payments.

Examples:

  • Visa
  • Mastercard
  • Gift Cards
  • Mobile Wallets

In One Line Each

  • POS: transaction execution
  • OMS: online order orchestration
  • IMS: inventory truth and stock state
  • ERP: accounting and finance posting
  • CRM/Loyalty: customer behavior and rewards
  • Payments: authorization, capture, settlement

System Of Record Vs System Of Engagement

CategoryExamplesPrimary Purpose
System of RecordERP, IMS, CatalogTrusted master data and auditable state
System of EngagementPOS, E-commerce UI, Loyalty AppCustomer and operator interaction
System of OrchestrationOMS, Payment GatewayCross-system coordination and workflow control
Design principle

Do not duplicate business truth in every system. Define one owning system per critical domain object.

checkpoint.prompt: OMS vs IMS in one line?
checkpoint.answer: OMS manages order lifecycle; IMS manages inventory state.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: POS Dependencies
chapters.content:
Common misconception

Many developers think POS works alone. It does not.

Upstream Dependencies

Systems POS depends on.

  • Price Service
  • Inventory Service
  • Tax Service
  • Promotion Service
  • Product Catalog
  • Loyalty Service

Example

Price Service Failure

Impact:

  1. Wrong Prices
  2. Customer Complaints
  3. Sales Loss

Downstream Dependencies

Systems depending on POS.

  • Reporting
  • ERP
  • Inventory Updates
  • Settlement
  • Analytics
  • Fraud Detection

Example

POS Transaction Not Uploaded

Impact:

  1. Inventory Drift
  2. Incorrect Sales Reports
  3. Reconciliation Issues

Example Impacts

  • Price service failure -> wrong prices, complaints, sales loss
  • Transaction upload failure -> inventory drift, reporting errors, reconciliation issues

Dependency Failure Matrix

DependencyTypical SymptomImmediate Mitigation
Price ServiceUnexpected totalsFallback to approved emergency price list
Tax ServiceTax mismatch warningsTrigger regional tax-rule fallback and audit queue
Loyalty ServicePoints not appliedIssue deferred benefit token for later reconciliation
Upload PipelineMissing transactions in HQReplay queue with idempotency keys
Operational insight

POS resilience is less about one perfect service and more about controlled degradation with clear reconciliation paths.

checkpoint.prompt: Price service down, POS up. What happens?
checkpoint.answer: Checkout may continue with wrong/stale prices, causing overrides and revenue leakage.

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Online vs Offline vs Omnichannel
chapters.content:
Offline Retail

Customer visits store.

Flow:

  1. Customer
  2. Store
  3. POS
Customer → Store → POS

Characteristics:

  • Immediate fulfillment
  • Store inventory
  • Cash payments possible

Online Retail

Customer orders digitally.

Flow:

  1. Website
  2. OMS
  3. Warehouse
  4. Shipping
  5. Customer

Characteristics:

  • Delivery delay
  • Fulfillment complexity
  • Shipping costs

Omnichannel Retail

Combines online and physical operations.

Examples:

PatternHow it worksMeaning
BOPIS
  • Buy Online
  • Pick Up In Store
Buy online, pick up in store
Ship From StoreStore inventory used to satisfy online orderStore inventory fulfills online order
Return To StoreOnline purchase returned physicallyOnline purchase returned physically

Capability Comparison

ModelStrengthComplexity Driver
OfflineImmediate fulfillmentIn-store staffing and queue control
OnlineWider reach and assortmentFulfillment and last-mile shipping
OmnichannelCustomer convenience and flexibilityReal-time inventory and order sync

checkpoint.prompt: Why is omnichannel harder to run?
checkpoint.answer: It requires cross-system synchronization between orders, inventory, and fulfillment.

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Real-World Scenario
chapters.content:
Scenario

A promotion is active.

Customer buys:

2 x Shampoo

Expected:

Buy One Get One Free
What actually happened

But discount not applied.

Question:

Which system might be failing?

Possible Answers:

  • Promotion Service ✅
  • POS Integration ✅
  • Pricing Feed ✅

Business Impact:

  • Customer complaints
  • Manual overrides
  • Revenue reporting inconsistencies

Triage Runbook

  1. Confirm promotion configuration: SKU scope, store scope, start/end time, channel eligibility.
  2. Validate customer/basket conditions: quantity threshold, excluded combinations, loyalty requirements.
  3. Inspect POS logs for rule evaluation response and fallback behavior.
  4. Compare expected vs actual price events in transaction audit trail.
  5. Escalate with incident template including sample receipt and transaction ID.

Recovery Options

  • Temporary cashier override policy with reason codes.
  • Back-office compensation coupon for affected customers.
  • Post-incident replay validation for reporting consistency.

checkpoint.answer: Validate promotion eligibility and validity for SKU/store/time.

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Quick Quiz
chapters.content:
Quick Quiz

Choose one answer for each question. The correct answer is marked with (Correct).

Q1

Which system is primarily responsible for inventory tracking?

  • A. CRM
  • B. IMS (Correct)
  • C. ERP
  • D. POS

Q2

What is an upstream dependency of POS?

  • A. ERP
  • B. Analytics
  • C. Pricing Service (Correct)
  • D. Reporting

Q3

Which system handles online order orchestration?

  • A. OMS (Correct)
  • B. CRM
  • C. POS
  • D. ERP

Q4

What comes after authorization in a payment lifecycle?

  • A. Inventory
  • B. Settlement
  • C. Capture (Correct)
  • D. Loyalty

Q5

Why does hierarchy matter during incidents?

  • A. It changes shelf labels
  • B. It sets blast radius and escalation ownership (Correct)
  • C. It removes tax complexity
  • D. It reduces card declines

checkpoint.prompt: What should you revisit if your score is low?
checkpoint.answer: Revisit system responsibilities, dependency flow, and KPI impact mapping.

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Practical Assignments
chapters.content:
Practical Assignment 1

Create:

domain/retail-system-map.md

Include:

  • All systems
  • Ownership
  • Data flows
  • Upstream dependencies
  • Downstream dependencies

Practical Assignment 2

Create:

domain/store-operating-model.md

Include:

  • Retail hierarchy
  • Store roles
  • Daily operations
  • Opening procedures
  • Closing procedures
  • Incident ownership matrix

Assignment Quality Checklist

  • Each system must include owned data entities and non-owned consumed entities.
  • Each dependency must include failure symptom and fallback approach.
  • Each store process must include role owner, timing, and observable output.
  • Incident matrix must define severity, escalation path, and communication SLA.
Why these are valuable

They convert domain theory into operational artifacts that speed up incident triage.

checkpoint.prompt: What makes these assignments high value?
checkpoint.answer: They convert domain theory into operational artifacts that speed up incident triage.
